text:
QUEEN’S
BENCH FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation:

2017 SKQB 326

Date:

201
7 10 30

Docket:
QBG 483 of 2016

Judicial
Centre:
Regina

BETWEEN:

FRANCES
FORSBERG, MONTANA CHARLES

FORSBERG, RENN WILLOW
FORSBERG,

CASSIDY ALLEN, DUSTIN DYCK, LUCAS DYCK,

MEGAN CHEESBROUGH, IAN MICHAEL JENSEN,

NOAH JENSEN

PLAINTIFFS

- and -

HER MAJESTY THE
QUEEN, IN RIGHT OF THE

PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN

DEFENDANT

CORRECTED
JUDGMENT:
The text of the original judgment has been
changed
per
the corrigendum released December 14, 2017. (A copy of the
corrigendum is appended to this corrected judgment.)

Counsel:

Larry
Kowalchuk/Micah Kowalchuk
for
the plaintiffs

Barbara Mysko
for
the Crown

DECISION
PRITCHARD
J.

OCTOBER 30, 2017

[
1
]

Two
applications have been made regarding an amended statement of claim [Action] in
which the plaintiffs allege that
ss. 31(1)
of
The
Vital Statistics Act, 2009
,
SS 2009, c V-7.21 [
Act
] is discriminatory. The impugned provision
states:

(2) An
individual who is at least 18 years of age and whose birth is registered in
Saskatchewan may apply to the registrar to have the designation of sex on the individual’s
statement amended by providing the following to the registrar:

(a) an
application in a form approved by the registrar;

(b) a statutory
declaration made by the applicant, in a form approved by the registrar, stating
that the applicant has assumed, identifies with and intends to maintain the
gender identity that corresponds with the requested amendment to the
designation of sex on the applicant’s statement;

(c) subject to subsection (3), a
letter from a health care professional practising in Saskatchewan or in another
province or territory of Canada:

(i) stating that:

(A) the health
care professional has treated or evaluated the applicant;

(B) in the
health care professional’s opinion, the applicant has assumed, identifies with
and is maintaining the gender identity that corresponds with the requested
amendment to the designation of sex on the applicant’s statement; and

(C) in the
health care professional’s opinion, the change of sex designation on the
applicant’s statement is appropriate; and

(ii) containing
any other information required by the registrar;

(d) the fee set by the
corporation.

The current version of ss. 31(1) results from amendments made in 2016
that introduced a procedure by which individuals whose birth is registered in
the Province of Saskatchewan may change the sex designation on their “statement”
or birth certificate. The provision is only available to those 18 years of age and
requires applicants to identify as either female or male. The requested change
in gender identification must also be supported by the written endorsement of a
medical professional.

[
2
]

The
plaintiffs maintain that the age restriction, as well as the requirements to
designate gender and to provide medical support for the change of gender offend
several provisions of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

[
Charter
]
and
The
Saskatchewan

Human Rights Code
, SS 1979, c S-24.1 [
Code
].
They therefore seek judicial relief under both the
Charter
and the
Code

including,
inter alia
, a declaration that the
Act
,
in particular

ss. 31(2), violates various specified sections of the
Charter
and the
Code
.

[
3
]

The parties
agree that the Action does not simply reference the
Code
in support of
its
Charter

claims. Rather, it is comprised of two independent parallel
claims: a claim that the
Act
offends the
Charter
and thus certain
remedies are appropriate; and a separate and independent claim that the
Act

offends the
Code
and thus other remedies as outlined in the
Code

are appropriate.

[
4
]

The
Province of Saskatchewan [Saskatchewan] has applied to strike all portions of the
Action that claim relief under the
Code

as disclosing no reasonable
claim. The plaintiffs had originally made the same claim against the
Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission [SHRC], as co-defendant, but the Action
has now been discontinued as against the SHRC.

[
5
]

The
plaintiffs have countered with an interlocutory application seeking,
inter
alia
, an interim order staying operation of the age and other restrictions
under
ss. 31(1)
of the
Act
including the requirement that there be a
male or female gender identification on issued or amended birth certificates. A
defence has not been filed by Saskatchewan pending the court’s determination of
these two applications. The parties agreed that the applications be heard
concurrently.

THE APPLICATION TO STRIKE

Position of Saskatchewan

[
6
]

Saskatchewan
applies for an order striking all portions of the Action that claimed relief
based solely on the
Code
including any remedies sought by the plaintiffs
that arise under the
Code
[
Code
claims]. The application is made
on the enumerated grounds set out in Rules 7-9(1) and 7-9(2) of
The Queen’s
Bench Rules
. The primary position of Saskatchewan is that because the Action
was not brought before the court through the process authorized under the
Code
,
the court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the
Code
claims.
Saskatchewan’s ancillary position is that the
Code
claims should be
stricken as an abuse of process because many of the plaintiffs have filed
parallel human rights complaints which are still pending or ongoing. It also
maintains that the
Code
claims are redundant in that they merely
duplicate the
Charter

claims made in the Action. Finally, Saskatchewan
submits that the
Code
claim seeking an order requiring the province to
fund a public education program should be stricken because specific performance
is not an available remedy.

[
7
]

The
submission by Saskatchewan that this Court does not have jurisdiction to
adjudicate alleged infractions of the
Code
outside the process directed
by the
Code
is based on
s. 29.6
of the
Code
. It states:

29.6(1) At any time after a complaint is
filed or initiated pursuant to section 27, the Chief Commissioner may apply to
the court for a hearing of the complaint at the judicial centre nearest to the
place where the subject-matter of the complaint arose.

(2) If the Chief Commissioner applies for a
hearing pursuant to subsection (1), the Chief Commissioner shall serve the
person against whom the complaint was made with a copy of the application.

[
8
]

Section
29.6 gives the court jurisdiction to conduct “hearings” dealing with alleged
infringements of the
Code
. These hearings were originally overseen by
the now defunct Saskatchewan Human Rights Tribunal. Under s. 29.6 of the
Code
,
these hearings are now held by the court but only after a complaint has been
made to the SHRC in accordance with s. 27 of the
Code
and the Chief
Commissioner has applied for a hearing to be held. It is common ground that the
Action does not constitute a hearing before the court as authorized under s.
29.6. Therefore, a determination as to whether the court has jurisdiction to
hear
Code
claims outside the process authorized under s. 29.6 is fundamental
to determining if the
Code
claims should be struck.

[
9
]

Saskatchewan
submits that the
Code
does not create civil causes of action and consequently,
alleged breaches of the
Code
are only actionable through the process
outlined in the
Code
. Saskatchewan therefore maintains that all relief
sought by the plaintiffs based on breaches of or remedies arising under the
Code

should be stricken. In support, it cites
Seneca College v Bhadauria
,

1981 CanLII 29 (SCC)
,
[1981] 2 SCR 181
[
Seneca
]
.
In
Seneca
, the Supreme Court unequivocally
held that the
Ontario Human Rights Code
,
RSO 1970, c 318 (since rep) [
Ontario
Code
] creates no civil causes of action and alleged breaches thereof are
actionable only through the Ontario’s Human Rights complaint process.
Saskatchewan submits that the
Code
is functionally identical to the
Ontario legislation
considered in
Seneca
and should be followed in these
proceedings.

[
10
]

Saskatchewan
also relies on
Lawless v Conseil Scolaire Fransaskois
,
2014 SKQB 23
,
436
Sask R 196
[
Lawless
]
.
In
Lawless
, the eldest son of the Lawless
family was attending a school administered by a Francophone school division.
The child was English speaking and was only permitted to attend on the basis of
a specially granted permission. The child was also autistic and had many severe
behavioural issues which eventually resulted in the school division deciding
not to renew its permission for him to attend the school. The family sought,
among other remedies, a declaration that the school violated sections of the
Code
.
The school division
relied on
Seneca
and applied to strike the action
insofar as it sought a declaration that
Code
provisions had been
violated. Justice Ball applied
Seneca
and struck the alleged
Code

breaches on the basis that the underlying issues could only be heard by the
court upon an application by the Chief Commissioner through the process
outlined under
s. 29.6
of the
Code
. In so doing, he stated at paras. 54
and 55:

54  The proposition that the only way to
enforce the provisions of the
Code
is to follow the process set out in
the
Code
itself has been consistently applied by courts in Saskatchewan.
See:
Battlefords and District Co-operative Ltd. v. Gibbs and Human Rights
Commission (Sask.)
,
(1994)
1994 CanLII 4550 (SK CA)
,
120 Sask. R. 166
; 116 D.L.R. (4th) 109 (Sask.
C.A.) per Jackson J.A., at para. 48;
Yorkton Union Hospital v. Saskatchewan
Union of Nurses,

1993 CanLII 6637 (SK CA)
,
[1993] 7 W.W.R. 129
,
109 Sask R 198 (Sask. C.A.)
per
Sherstobitoff J.A. at para. 76;
Ingold v. Rural Municipality of Wheatlands
No. 163
,
2004 SKQB 178
,
251 Sask.R. 75
per Matheson J. at para. 44. In
Cadillac
Fairview Corp. v. Saskatchewan (Board of Inquiry)
,
1999 CanLII 12358 (SK CA)
,
[1999] 7 W.W.R. 517
,
177
Sask. R. 126 (Sask. C.A.)
, Vancise J.A. stated at para. 32:

32 ... It has long been established that
human rights codes foreclose any cause of action at common law for a violation
of the fundamental principles which are guaranteed by the
Code
and that
the only method of enforcement of the substantive rights based upon a breach of
the provisions of the
Code
is the complaint procedure section in the
Code

itself. Any action in the courts based on public policy was also foreclosed.
...

55  Since there can be no action at common
law to address alleged violations of the
Code
, the court's jurisdiction
must be found created by statute,
i.e.
by the
Code
itself.
Recently enacted provisions of the
Code
state that the court's authority
to hear and determine the underlying issues raised by a complaint to the SHRC
arise upon an application for a hearing to be made by the SHRC's Chief
Commissioner pursuant to
s. 29.6
of the
Code
.

Position of the plaintiffs

[
11
]

The
plaintiffs respond with a number of assertions. First, they submit that a cause
of action alleging a breach of the
Code
can proceed before the court if
it also contains human rights concerns based on a separate and distinct cause
of action, such as a violation of the
Charter
. Second, the plaintiffs
submit that the
Code
itself does not specifically state that the SHRC has
sole jurisdiction over any matter or proceedings that triggers a
Code

provision. In essence, the plaintiffs maintain that alleged infractions of the
Code

can be tried by the court outside the limited process directed by the
Code.

In support, the plaintiffs rely on
the decision of Justice Ball in
R v
Whatcott
,
2002 SKQB 399
,
225 Sask R 205
[
Whatcott
]
.

[
12
]

In
Whatcott
,
Justice Ball rejected,
in obiter
, the argument that only a board of
inquiry established under the
Code
has jurisdiction to declare a law to
be inoperative by reason of it contravening the
Code
. Justice Ball found
that, in certain circumstances, the court has jurisdiction to consider and
apply provisions of the
Code
outside the process outlined therein. The
court’s reasons for assuming jurisdiction
in
Whatcott
are set out in
para.
34
where Justice Ball states:

34  The situation here is quite different
[from
Seneca
]. The appellant in this case is not pursuing a remedy
against the University. On the contrary, the University is pursuing a remedy
against the appellant. The University chose to charge the appellant with an
offence under its Bylaw which specified that it was to be enforceable in
Provincial Court. The appellant wishes to rely on the defence that the Bylaw is
rendered inoperative by legislation, namely,
s. 44
of The
Saskatchewan Human
Rights Code
. He is not required to pursue his defence in another forum by filing
a complaint with The Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission, nor to ask that a
board of inquiry be established by the Commission to decide whether he has a
defence to the charge being tried by the Court.

[
13
]

I am satisfied
that
Whatcott
is of no assistance to the plaintiffs. To the contrary,
the explicitness of Justice Ball’s reasons for
distinguishing
Whatcott

from
Seneca
and thereby assuming jurisdiction supports Saskatchewan’s
position that
Whatcott
cannot and should not be broadly construed. The
essence of
Whatcott
is that the court has jurisdiction to consider and
apply provisions of the
Code
outside the process outlined by the
Code

where such adjudication is necessary to assess a defence. The decision is based
on the important distinction that the plaintiff in
Whatcott
was not
pursuing a remedy under the
Code
and in such circumstances, it was up to
the court and not the SHRC to determine if the defence was valid.

[
14
]

The
plaintiffs also rely on
Billinkoff v Winnipeg School Division No. 1
,

1999 CanLII 14067 (MB CA)
,
[1999] 7 WWR 489 (Man CA)
[
Billinkoff
]
and
Sparrow v The
Manufacturers Life Insurance Co.
,
2004 MBQB 281
,
206 Man R (2d) 1
. These
two cases come from a line of Manitoba jurisprudence [Manitoba Cases] that
directly contradict
Seneca
and
Lawless
and, if applied
, would
support the plaintiffs’ position that the court can adjudicate alleged
infractions of the
Code
outside the process directed by the
Code
.

[
15
]

In
Billinkoff
,
the plaintiff teachers appealed the dismissal of their application for a
declaration that certain provincial regulations and collective agreements were
unconstitutional in that they did not provide for paid days off for the
observance of Jewish holidays. The motions court had dismissed the applications
on the basis of jurisdiction. On appeal, the Manitoba Court of Appeal
distinguished Manitoba’s human rights legislation from the Ontario legislation
on which
Seneca
was based. It determined it was appropriate for the
court to also hear the parallel complaint by the teachers of a failure on the
part of their employer to make reasonable accommodation as required by the
Human
Rights Code
,
CCSM, c H175 [
Manitoba Code
]. It therefore concluded that “the
motions judge was in error in concluding that ‘complaints under the Human
Rights Code should be processed in accordance with the provisions of the Human Rights
Code.’” and ordered that “the applications be consolidated and proceed ahead in
the Court of Queen’s Bench.” (para. 54)

[
16
]

The
decision in
Billinkoff
was based primarily on the seminal Manitoba
decision of
Parkinson v Health Sciences Centre

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2908 (MB CA)
,
13 Man R (2d) 233
(Man CA)
[
Parkinson
]

where the Manitoba Court of Appeal distinguished
Seneca
on the basis of
the statutory difference between the
Ontario Code
and the
Manitoba
Code
.

[
17
]

Parkinson
was decided in 1982, one
year after the Supreme Court of Canada released
Seneca
.
In
Parkinson
,
a doctor challenged a mandatory retirement age on the basis that it offended
the former
Human Rights Act, 1974
(Man), c 65 (since rep)

in
effect at that time [
Old

Manitoba Code
]. The plaintiff doctor
sought a declaration that the mandatory retirement age contravened the
Old Manitoba
Code
although he did not seek damages. Taking great pains to distinguish
the case before it from
Seneca
, the Manitoba Court of Appeal ultimately
concluded that the
Old

Manitoba Code
did not preclude an
alternative action based on an alleged infraction of that code and agreed to
grant declaratory relief. The basis for
distinguishing
Seneca
was
two-fold.
In
Seneca
, the plaintiff commenced an action “in the usual
sense” and pursued damages, whereas
in
Parkinson
, the plaintiff only
sought a declaratory order. The Manitoba Court of Appeal determined that the
court had very broad discretion to grant declaratory orders. Also, the wording
of s. 34 of the
Old Manitoba Code
in effect at that time was different
from the
Ontario Code
on which
Seneca
was based. Section 34 of the

Old Manitoba Code
stated:

34.In addition to what may be permitted by
this
Act
, a person who deprives, abridges or otherwise restricts or attempts to
deprive, abridge or otherwise restricts a person or class of persons in the
enjoyment of a right under this Act because of the race, nationality, religion,
colour, sex, age, marital status, physical handicap, ethnic or national origin,
political belief, family status, or source of income of the person; may be
restrained by an injunction issued in an action in the Court of Queen's Bench
brought by any person against the person responsible for the deprivation,
abridgement or other restriction or any attempt thereat.

[
18
]

The
Manitoba Court of Appeal therefore concluded that the unique breadth of
jurisdiction afforded Manitoba courts under s. 34 gave the courts in Manitoba
more general jurisdiction to adjudicate human rights actions than afforded to
Ontario courts.

ANALYSIS

[
19
]

There
is conflicting jurisprudence on the central issue of the court’s jurisdiction
to hear the
Code
claims in the Action. Saskatchewan
relies on the
Seneca
/
Lawless

cases,
the plaintiffs rely upon the Manitoba Cases. Rational arguments have
been made on both sides.

Argument Manitoba Cases Should Prevail

[
20
]

Perhaps
the most persuasive reason to follow the Manitoba Cases is that
ss. 38(3)
of
the
Code

relating to injunctions is more akin to the
Old Manitoba
Code
than to the
Ontario Code
.
Section 38(3)
states:

38
(3) The commission or any person may, by statement of
claim, commence an action in the court against any person for an injunction to
restrain the person:

(a) from depriving, abridging or otherwise
restricting or attempting to deprive, abridge or restrict a person or a class
of persons in the enjoyment of a right pursuant to this
Act
or any other Act
administered by the commission; or

(b) from contravening or attempting to
contravene any provision of this
Act
or any other Act administered by the
commission.

[
21
]

The
Ontario
Code
at the time
Seneca
was decided provided a very limited right to
apply for an injunction. Under the
Ontario Code
, an applicant could only
apply for an injunction to restrain the continuance of a violation of the
Ontario
Code
. As such, injunctions were only available after an Ontario Human
Rights Tribunal had already found a violation of the
Ontario Code
. In
contrast to the
Ontario Code
, s. 34 of the
Old Manitoba Code
gave
any person immediate access to the courts, without the necessity of going
through the process of filing a human rights complaint and having the commission
deal with the complaint as set forth in the legislation. This differentiation
was essential to the decision of the Manitoba Court of Appeal’s
decision in
Parkinson

to not follow
Seneca
.

[
22
]

Although
the question of whether injunctive relief under
ss. 38(3)
of the
Code
is
available in Saskatchewan without first going through the process of filing a
human rights complaint has been questioned (and will be discussed later in this
decision) on its face, it seems to be so. This suggests that, as
in
Parkinson
,
the relevant provision of the
Code

is distinguishable from the provision
on which
Seneca
was based and that accordingly, the Manitoba Cases may
be more applicable than
Seneca
.

[
23
]

The
Code

also lacks the exclusive jurisdiction clause relied on
in
Seneca
. At 186-187
of
Seneca,
the Supreme Court reviewed the applicable Ontario legislation
and stated:

…Under s. 14
b
(6), a board of inquiry
(subject to the provisions of s. 14
d
, respecting appeals) “has exclusive
jurisdiction and authority to determine any question of fact or law or both
required to be decided in reaching a decision as to whether or not any person
has contravened this
Act
or for the making of any order pursuant to such decision”.

[
24
]

The
Supreme Court went on to reference “the comprehensiveness of the
Code
in its
administrative and adjudicative features, the latter including a wide right of
appeal to the courts on both fact and law”. It is undisputed that the
Code
has
no equivalent provision to ss. 14(b)(6) of the Ontario legislation. This also
suggests that the Manitoba Cases should be persuasive.

Argument Seneca/Lawless Should Prevail

[
25
]

The
main argument for Saskatchewan’s position that
Seneca/Lawless
should be
followed is that regardless of the previously discussed statutory differences,
Seneca

has always been applied in Saskatchewan. Unlike Manitoba courts which
essentially abandoned
Seneca
within a year of its release, the
Saskatchewan Court of Appeal immediately applied it. This is first seen in
Kodellas
v Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission)

(1989),
1989 CanLII 284 (SK CA)
,
77 Sask R 94 (CA)
where
the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal stated:

42      … The only forum available to the
complainants to compensate them for the injury caused them (should it be found
that they suffered injury) is [through the Human Rights complaint process]. To
deprive them of an inquiry is to deprive them of their only access to justice. The
Supreme Court of Canada authoritatively removed any doubt that existed in this
regard when it
decided
Seneca
College of Applied Arts and Technology v.
Badhauria
. …

[
26
]

The
Saskatchewan Court of Appeal expressed the same sentiment
in
Cadillac
Fairview Corp. Ltd. v Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission)

(1999),
1999 CanLII 12358 (SK CA)
,
177
Sask R 126 (CA)
:

32      …It has long been established that human
rights codes foreclose any cause of action at common law for a violation of the
fundamental principles which are guaranteed by the
Code
and that the
only method of enforcement of the substantive rights based upon a breach of the
provisions of the
Code
is the complaint procedure section in the
Code

itself.  Any action in the courts based on public policy was also
foreclosed. …

[
27
]

The
Seneca

approach
has continued to be applied in Saskatchewan regardless of the
abolition of the Human Rights Tribunal and the addition of
ss. 38(3)
to the
Code
.

Lawless
and
Lapchuk v Saskatchewan
,

2015 SKQB 358
,
468
Sask R 170
are decisions of Justice Ball that represent two recent such
examples.
In
Lawless
, Justice Ball noted at para. 53 that
Seneca

“has never been overruled” and at para. 54 that “[t]he proposition that the
only way to enforce the provisions of the
Code
is to follow the process
set out in the
Code
itself has been consistently applied by courts in
Saskatchewan”.

[
28
]

Given
the long history of
applying
Seneca
in Saskatchewan, I am convinced that

Seneca/Lawless
rather than the Manitoba Cases should be followed in this
instance. Accordingly,
based on
Seneca
/Lawless
, I conclude that this
Court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate alleged infractions of the
Code

outside the process directed by the
Code
. (The only qualifier, as
subsequently discussed, is if the matter relates to a claim for injunctive
relief made pursuant to
ss. 38(3)
of the
Code
.)

[
29
]

In
coming to this conclusion, I have not discussed the other arguments made by the
plaintiffs as they do not affect the outcome. The first is the submission that
a statement of claim can rely on
Code
provisions for the purpose of
bolstering or supporting an independent cause of action. This is not relevant
because the Action does not simply reference the
Code
to bolster its
Charter

claims but makes two independent parallel claims; one, that the
Act

offends the
Charter
and thus certain remedies are appropriate and the
other that the
Act
offends the
Code
and thus other remedies
outlined in the
Code
are appropriate. Saskatchewan has only taken issue
with the claims founded on the
Code
provisions, not on the plaintiffs’
ability to reference the
Code
provisions in an effort to establish the
Charter

claims.

[
30
]

The
Ontario Court of Appeal decision in
L’Attiboudeaire v Royal Bank of Canada

(1996),
1996 CanLII 1411 (ON CA)
,
131 DLR (4
th
) 445 (Ont CA)
[
L’Attiboudeaire
]
, relied
on by the plaintiffs actually illustrates the distinction between claims based
on the human rights legislation and claims supported by it.
In
L’Attiboudeaire
,
the pleadings are discussed at 446:

The plaintiff alleges that he is a young
male person of African-Caribbean origin "and that, but for such
attributions, he would not have been treated as aforesaid."

In paragraphs 13 and 14 of the statement
of claim he alleges:

13.The Plaintiff states that but for the
conduct of the defendant as aforesaid, he would have continued in his
employment and that such conduct therefore resulted in his constructive
dismissal.

14.The Plaintiff further states that the
conduct of the defendant as described above is in contravention of both the
defendant's own policy on harassment, its Code of Conduct as well as the
Canadian Human Rights Act. The defendant [sic., the plaintiff?) will rely upon
such policy, Code and Act as conclusive proof of community standards in
assessing whether or not the conduct of the defendant was wrongful.

[
31
]

The
pleadings
in
L’Attiboudeaire
allege wrongful dismissal and seek remedies for wrongful
dismissal. The relevant
Ontario Code
is referenced only as a factor to
consider in determining whether the “conduct of the defendant was wrongful”. However,
the
Code

claims in the Action are different as the alleged
Code
violations
are relied upon as the foundation for an independent cause of action. The
Ontario Court of Appeal decision (at 447) shows that this distinction is
central to its decision. It states:

…the cause of action alleged
in [
L’Attiboudeaire
]
is not based upon a breach of the Canadian Human Rights Act … The plaintiff in
the present case had been in an employment relationship with the defendant and,
in order to prove conduct on the part of the defendant which amounted to
constructive dismissal (generally, a fundamental breach of the terms of the
employment contract) he does not need to invoke the policy of the Canadian
Human Rights Act. This does not mean that its terms could not be relevant
factors to take into account in assessing the defendant's conduct.

Likewise,
Westfair Foods Ltd. v Lippens Inc.

(1989),
1989 CanLII 5257 (MB CA)
,
64 DLR (4
th
)
335 (Man CA)
;
Thomas v Woolworth Canada Inc.
(1996),
9 OTC 123 (Ont Ct
J)
; and
Macaraeg v E Care Contact Centers Ltd.
,
2006 BCSC 1851
,
[2007] 1
WWR 421
, also cited by the plaintiffs, are not applicable for the same reasons.

[
32
]

The
plaintiffs have also argued that a civil action and human rights action
grounded in the same alleged wrong can be filed concurrently. This may be so,
but it is simply not relevant to a determination as to whether the court has
jurisdiction to determine alleged infractions of the
Code
outside the
process directed by the
Code
.

[
33
]

The
plaintiffs referred to
McKinley v BC Tel

(1996),
23 BCLR (3d) 367 (BCSC)

[
McKinley
]
as an example of an alleged wrong forming the basis of both a
civil action (the civil action was a wrongful dismissal claim) and a human
rights complaint based on discrimination. In
McKinley
, the defendant
sought a stay of the civil action on the basis that the relevant Human Rights
Tribunal had exclusive jurisdiction to hear complaints founded on
discrimination. The court refused the application as the allegation that the
defendant breached the human rights legislation was incidential to breach of
the employment contract. This decision is immaterial to this proceeding because
Saskatchewan has conceded that the court has jurisdiction to hear the
Charter

claims in the Action and only seeks an order striking the
Code
claims.

[
34
]

The
plaintiffs similarly refer to
ss. 27.1(1)
,
27.1(2)
(d) and
27.1(3)
of the
Code

to show that the
Code’s
drafters contemplated parallel civil and human
rights actions proceeding from the same alleged wrong. The most relevant is
s.
27.1(3)
which states:

27
(3)  The Chief Commissioner may, at any time after a
complaint is filed or initiated, defer further action if another proceeding, in
the opinion of the Chief Commissioner, is more appropriate having regard to the
nature of the allegations and the remedies available in the other proceeding.

Saskatchewan submits that the referenced provisions only demonstrate that
the SHRC does not have exclusive jurisdiction to hear complaints founded on
discrimination and says that is why it has conceded that the same matter can
proceed both as a civil action and human rights complaint but only where there
exists an independent cause of action to ground the civil action. I agree. In
my view,
McKinley
and the above referenced provisions of the
Code

only demonstrate that
Charter
claims cannot be dismissed on the grounds
that they are founded on discrimination. However, they do not stand for the
notion that the court has original jurisdiction to determine alleged
infractions of the
Code
outside the process directed by the
Code
.
And, as stated, the essence of these authorities is simply not relevant as
Saskatchewan has not asked that any of the
Charter
claims be stricken.

[
35
]

Based
on the foregoing, the claims made under paras. 49(5), (6), (7) and (8) of the
Action are struck as disclosing no reasonable action. The striking of these
paragraphs from the “Remedy” portion of the Action requires a striking of the
corresponding references and allegations based on the
Code
, sprinkled
throughout, and include the following paragraphs and parts thereof:

All of paragraph 22

All of paragraph 23

All of paragraph 24

All of paragraph 25

All of paragraph 26

Reference to the
Code
in paragraph 28

Reference to the
Code
in paragraph 39

All of paragraph 48

Once an amended claim is served and filed in accordance with this
decision, the defendant shall be in a position to file its defence. I now turn
to the plaintiffs’ injunction application.

APPLICATION FOR INJUNCTIONS

[
36
]

The
plaintiffs have applied for the following interlocutory orders:

1.

An interim
order staying operation of that portion of

ss. 31(2)
of the
Act
that states “who is at least 18 years of age”;

2.

An interim
order removing the requirement for gender and/or sex designation in various
enumerated provisions of the
Act
and regulations enacted pursuant to
s.
104
of the
Act
.

[
37
]

I have
already determined that the court does not have jurisdiction to adjudicate
alleged contraventions of the
Code
outside the process set out in the
Code
.
The plaintiffs’ interlocutory application raises a distinct but related
question; namely, does the court have jurisdiction to grant injunctive relief
related to alleged contraventions of the
Code
even though it does not
have jurisdiction to hear and determine the underlying human rights complaints?
If answered in the affirmative, the preceding decision that alleged infractions
of the
Code
must be struck will not prevent the court from adjudicating
the injunction application under the
Code
.

[
38
]

The
plaintiffs submit
ss. 38(3)
of the
Code
confers jurisdiction on the
court to consider their application for injunction under the
Code
even
if the
Code
claims are struck. Section 38 has previously been quoted but
I will do so again for ease of reference:

Injunction

38
(1)
Where a person has been convicted of an offence under this
Act
or any other Act
administered by the commission, the commission may apply by way of notice of motion
to a judge of the court for an order enjoining that person from continuing or repeating
the offence, and the judge may make any order that the judge considers fit.

(2) Any order
made under subsection (1) may be enforced in the same manner as any other order
or judgment of the court.

(3) The
commission or any person may, by statement of claim, commence an action in the
court against any person for an injunction to restrain the person:

(a) from
depriving, abridging or otherwise restricting or attempting to deprive, abridge
or restrict a person or a class of persons in the enjoyment of a right pursuant
to this
Act
or any other Act administered by the commission; or

(b) from
contravening or attempting to contravene any provision of this
Act
or any other
Act administered by the commission.

(3.1) In an
action pursuant to subsection (3), the judge may make any order that the judge
considers fit.

(4) An appeal
lies to the Court of Appeal from the order or decision of a judge made under
subsection (3).

[
39
]

Although
Saskatchewan focused its arguments on the appropriateness of the requested
injunctions, it also questioned the court’s jurisdiction under
ss. 38(3)
to
consider injunctive relief stemming from alleged contraventions of the
Code
.
Saskatchewan acknowledges that a plain reading of
ss. 38(3)
suggests a broad
and unqualified right to apply for an injunction remedy for alleged
contraventions of the
Code
. However, based on
ss. 38(3)
’s proximity to ss.
38(1), Saskatchewan argues for a more restrictive interpretation. It submits that

ss. 38(3)
should share ss. 38(1)’s qualifications on who may apply for an
injunction. It therefore maintains that the authority under
ss. 38(3)
for “any
person” to commence an action “for an injunction to restrain …” relates back to
the qualifier under ss. 38(1) so that an injunction is only available “where a person
has been convicted of an offence” under the
Act
.

[
40
]

The
plaintiffs argue for the plain reading of the words in ss. 38(3) that state “any
person may … commence an action in the court against any person for an
injunction.” They say that the words neither state nor suggest that injunctive
relief for an alleged contravention of the
Code
is contingent upon there
having been a previous conviction under the
Code
.

[
41
]

I acknowledge
Saskatchewan’s position that it is unusual that

ss. 38(1) and 38(3) would share a section and that the more expansive authority
under ss. 38(3), as argued for by the plaintiffs, would follow the more
restrictive one under ss. 38(1). Some support for Saskatchewan’s position is
found in the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Committee for the
Commonwealth of Canada v Canada
,
[1991] 1 SCR 139
at 159-160
. In that case,
the Supreme Court was asked to determine whether
s. 7
of the
Government
Airport Concession Operations Regulations
, SOR/79-373 applied only to
business or commercial advertising as opposed to political advertising. Section
7 of that regulation at that time stated:

7.  Subject to section 8, except as
authorized in writing by the Minister, no person shall

(a)

conduct any business or
undertaking, commercial or otherwise, at an airport;

(b)

advertise or solicit at
an airport on his own behalf or on behalf of any person; or

(c)

fix, install or place
anything in an airport for the purpose of any business or undertaking.

[
42
]

Read
in isolation, the plain meaning of
s. 7
does not appear to be restricted to
business or commercial activity. However, the court analysed

ss. 7(b) and concluded that, in its context, all of s. 7 dealt with commercial
operations.

[
43
]

Although
the plain meaning of
s. 38(3)
might seem incongruent when it follows ss. 38(1),
that meaning has been historically applied by Saskatchewan courts. The
subsection first received judicial attention in
Human Rights Commission
(Sask.) v Bell

(1991),
1991 CanLII 7733 (SK QB)
,
96 Sask R 296 (QB)
[
Bell
]
where the court
stated at para. 81:

81
In Manitoba, as in Saskatchewan, the right to injunctive
relief arises immediately under the
Act
, and is not merely a step in the
course of the enforcement procedures of the
Saskatchewan Code.
The
latter types of provisions exist in all human rights legislation in Canada.

[
44
]

The
decision was successfully appealed in Saskatchewan (
Human Rights Commission
(Sask.) v Bell

(1994),
1994 CanLII 4699 (SK CA)
,
120 Sask R 122 (CA)
but on other grounds. The
Saskatchewan Court of Appeal did not take issue, or even address, the lower
court’s interpretation of ss. 38(3).

[
45
]

Section
38(3) was next considered in
Grant v Saskatoon (City) Commissioners of
Police

(1995),
1995 CanLII 5766 (SK QB)
,
132 Sask R 157 (QB)
[
Grant
]
. In that case, an
employee applied for an injunction to restrain an employer from enforcing
mandatory retirement age on the grounds that it offended
ss. 16(1)
of the
Code
.
A human rights complaint had been filed but the employee was scheduled to be
forced to retire before the SHRC would have had time to process the complaint.
Although the court eventually dismissed the application, it assumed
jurisdiction to hear it, implicitly applying
ss. 38(3)
’s plain meaning.

[
46
]

Lawless
provides
the most
thorough discussion of
ss. 38(3)
’s applicability to date.
In
Lawless
,
Justice Ball assumed jurisdiction to hear the injunction application
notwithstanding that he had determined that he otherwise had no jurisdiction to
adjudicate complaints alleging violations of the
Code
without the matter
having been referred to the court pursuant to

s. 29.6
of the
Code
. In so doing, he accepted
ss. 38(3)
’s plain meaning,
stating at paras. 60-61:

60
In my view,
Section 38(3)
of the
Code
is not
intended to confer an original jurisdiction on the court to hear and determine
underlying issues in human rights complaints as an alternative to, or in a
manner that would bypass, the
Code
's other provisions for initiating,
investigating and attempting to settle those complaints. Until those processes
are followed and an application to the court is made pursuant to s. 26.9 [
sic
– 29.
6] of the
Code
, the court's jurisdiction does not arise. In the
interim, s. 38(3) of the
Code
confines the court's jurisdiction to
granting injunctive relief in appropriate circumstances.

61
I will add what may be self-evident. An applicant seeking
injunctive relief under
s. 38(3)
of the
Code
must satisfy the
established criteria for the granting of that relief. One of those criteria
involves a preliminary assessment of the merits to determine if there is a
serious issue to be tried. ...

[
47
]

At
para. 70, Justice Ball added that:

70
… the court's jurisdiction to [hear a matter deriving from
Human Rights complaints outside the process outlined in s. 29.6] … confined to
granting injunctive relief under
s. 38(3)
of the
Code
.

[
48
]

Although

Bell
,
Grant
and
Lawless
have each applied the plain
meaning of
ss. 38(3)
, it is noted that none of them specifically addressed the
apparent inconsistency between
ss. 38(3)
and 38(1). Nevertheless, these cases
provide precedent for the position that the plain meaning interpretation is appropriate.
They also suggest that, despite the apparent incongruity,
ss. 38(3)
is not
genuinely ambiguous to the point it merits the court departing from the
subsection’s plain meaning and relying on external interpretative aids.

[
49
]

As the
plain meaning of
ss. 38(3)
has historically been accepted, I will proceed on
that basis. Accordingly, I accept that
ss. 38(3)
of the
Act
confers
jurisdiction to adjudicate injunction applications stemming from alleged
contraventions of the
Code
even where the court does not have
jurisdiction to hear and determine the underlying human rights issues. Here, this
conclusion is important because the plaintiffs have not complied with the
notice provision of
s. 13
of
The

Constitutional Questions Act, 2012
,
SS 2012, c C-29.01 and are therefore not in a positon to seek interlocutory
injunctive relief regarding their
Charter

claims. Section 13 states:

Notice to
Attorneys General required for constitutional questions

13
No
court shall hold any law to be invalid, inapplicable or inoperable if a constitutional
question is raised nor shall it grant any remedy unless notice is served on the
Attorney General of Canada and on the Attorney General for Saskatchewan in
accordance with this Part.

[
50
]

Although
the court is not at this time in a position to grant interlocutory relief under
the
Charter
, it appears that the same considerations would generally apply
to the requested relief injunctive whether made under the
Code

or the
Charter
.

Should Interim Injunctive Relief be Granted
Under the Code?

[
51
]

Both
parties agree that the three considerations that the court must weigh in
determining whether to grant interlocutory injunctive relief are: (i) the
seriousness of the issues to be tried; (ii) the resulting irreparable harm if
the relief is not granted; and, (iii) an assessment of the balance of
inconvenience to the parties. However, Saskatchewan further submits that before
the court even considers this three-part test, it must determine whether the
specific relief being requested can correctly be ordered at this stage of the
proceedings.

[
52
]

Saskatchewan
maintains that there is no jurisdictional authority for a court to grant
interlocutory relief that essentially amounts to a legislative amendment. It says
that although the plaintiffs have described their interlocutory application as
seeking “interim orders”, in reality, the requested orders are more akin to
permanent injunctions.

[
53
]

The
plaintiffs seek two interim orders. The first requests a stay of “the operation
of the part of ss. 31(2) of
The Vital Statistics Act
which state who is at
least 18 years of age and”. Although the plaintiffs characterize this relief as
a “stay”, I agree that the effect of the requested “stay” amounts to a striking
out of the age limitation currently found in
ss. 31(2)
. Thus, insofar as each
plaintiff under age 18 is concerned, even an interim order striking out the
impugned words would potentially have the effect of striking them out on a
permanent basis. The plaintiffs have made it clear that they are seeking this interlocutory
relief to enable plaintiffs that are under age 18 to immediately seek changes
to their birth registrations without having to wait for the court to determine
if the age restriction under
ss. 31(2)
is valid or invalid. As such, the
requested “interim stay” would not merely maintain the
status quo
. It
would result in the court immediately granting the ultimate relief being sought
by the underage plaintiffs without the benefit of a trial on the issue.

[
54
]

Further,
the plaintiffs are not seeking an interlocutory order that simply restrains the
Director of Vital Statistics from acting on existing legislation pending
resolution of the action; they are seeking an order that requires the Director
to affirmatively act. The actual effect of the requested “stay” is that the
court would be requiring the Director to take steps to issue new and amended
birth certifications for under age plaintiffs and presumably any other
applicant now under age 18. Without the “interim stay”, the Director would have
no legal authority to issue amended birth certificates to plaintiffs now under
age 18. The court would then also be creating the additional issue of how birth
certificates amended during the interim stay should be dealt with if the
interim order is not subsequently upheld at trial. Will the documents amended
for underage plaintiffs be surrendered and, if so, and on what authority will
the documents amended during the stay be amended back to reflect original gender
identities?

[
55
]

The
second interlocutory order requested by the plaintiffs is equally if not more problematic.
If granted, the second interim order would remove the existing gender and/or
sex designation of either male or female wherever found in the
Act
. The
plaintiffs submit that this statutory requirement must immediately end as it is
a
prima facie
limitation on their freedom of expression. According to
the plaintiffs, requiring that a baby’s gender be noted on a birth certificate
is archaic and “rooted in past practice and previous societal norms, none of
which are relevant or necessary today”. That may be so, but without a full
trial and appreciation of the potentially sweeping consequences of such a
significant order, it would be irresponsible for this Court to entirely eliminate
the long-standing collection of gender information on all official statements,
registrations and certificates relating to vital human events throughout the province.

[
56
]

An
order deleting the statutory requirement for gender identification is not only premature
but too broad in its scope for an interim order. Even if the plaintiffs are
ultimately successful at trial, evidence at that time might satisfy the court
that Saskatchewan requires a period of time before it must comply with any
resulting orders. And, even if successful, the court might ultimately determine
that increasing the scope of options available may be an appropriate remedy
rather than requiring that male or female gender identification be entirely
eliminated as being requested by the plaintiffs.

[
57
]

I
accept Saskatchewan’s submission that both requested orders are effectively
mandatory and that each may also have permanent effect (amended birth
certificates being issued to non-adult plaintiffs and perhaps others;
inevitable gaps in vital provincial statistics without transitional
arrangements in place). Both requested interlocutory orders would require the
court to intrude into the legislative realm without the benefit of due process
that permits an extensive review of the merits of the competing interests
involved. Moreover, the plaintiffs have provided no authority for the court to
grant an interlocutory injunction that directly or indirectly effects
legislative change.

[
58
]

The
court accepts that the process of accomplishing legislative change that is more
reflective of society’s evolving recognitions and understandings of basic human
rights has been arduous for these plaintiffs. Nevertheless, it must deny the
requested injunctive relief. In so doing, it is noted that one obvious
impediment to Saskatchewan continuing to retain a statutory requirement for
gender identification limited to either male or female is the recent
announcement that the Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship
Canada will be the first Government of Canada department to allow people who do
not identify as female (F) or male (M) to identify as unspecified (X).

[
59
]

Costs
shall be in the cause.

J.
